ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Neurology (movement disorders) Consultation — Katharine Hepburn — True-date frame: synthetic events are moved into the patient's historical lifetime. Codes, instruments, and treatments remain modern and are anachronistic.

code.originalText: Four-week follow-up with movement disorders neurology consultation: diagnosis and choice of treatment

text.paragraph: Head, voice, and bilateral hand tremor in a 72-year-old woman, the hand tremor present for several years and the head tremor visible for at least a year and slowly worsening, which others have taken for Parkinson's disease. Please confirm the diagnosis, advise on treatment for the hand tremor that interferes with her daily tasks and stage work, and advise on the head and voice tremor. [S]
Urgency: Routine, within four weeks, on the same day as her four-week primary care check. [S]

list.item: Does she meet the MDS consensus criteria for essential tremor, and is there anything to suggest Parkinson's disease, dystonic tremor, or essential tremor plus that would call for imaging?
Which medicine do you recommend first, propranolol or primidone, at her age, and with what monitoring?
What can be offered for the head tremor and the voice tremor?
What rehabilitation or aids would help with eating, drinking, and writing?
At what point would focused ultrasound thalamotomy or deep brain stimulation be considered?
How often should she be followed, and by whom?

text.paragraph: Ms. Hepburn, a 72-year-old actress, is seen at the request of Dr. Price for a tremor of the head, voice, and hands. The head tremor has been visible for at least a year and has slowly worsened; it is side to side and settles when she rests her head against a high-backed chair. Her hands have shaken for several years when she carries a full cup, pours, writes, and signs her name, and she now carries cups half full. Her voice wavers on sustained notes on stage. She has no tremor of the hands at rest, no stiffness, slowness, shuffling, falls, numbness, or memory change. She takes no medicines, drinks one cup of coffee in the morning, and has no asthma. She says her grandfather's head and hand shook as well. [S]
Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: Katharine Hepburn was born in Hartford, Connecticut, on May 12, 1907. [D]
By the 1980s Hepburn had a noticeable tremor that left her head constantly shaking; it was noticeable by the time of a 1979 television film and worsened later in her life. [D]
An obituary described her famous voice in her last years as quivery. [D]

Her tremor is identified as essential tremor by an encyclopedia article, a public radio report, and a physician's newspaper column, all of which note that it was widely mistaken for Parkinson's disease; an Associated Press obituary described tremors similar to Parkinson's disease. No public statement by a physician who examined her was found. [R]

text.paragraph: No results recorded at this visit.

list.item: Essential tremor (G25.0). Essential tremor by the MDS consensus classification: an isolated action tremor of both upper limbs for more than three years, with head and voice tremor and no other neurological signs. There is no rest tremor, bradykinesia, or rigidity to suggest Parkinson's disease; no abnormal posture, head turning, or null point to suggest dystonic tremor; and no tandem-gait, memory, or other soft signs that would make it essential tremor plus. The reported family history fits. A dopamine transporter scan or brain MRI would add nothing. [S]

Choice of treatment. Propranolol and primidone are both established first-line treatments for limb tremor. At 72 she has no asthma, slow pulse, heart block, or diabetes, so propranolol is suitable and avoids the sedation, unsteadiness, and fall risk primidone carries at her age. The extended-release form allows one morning dose. [S]

Head and voice tremor (R49.8). Head and voice tremor respond less to medicines than hand tremor. Propranolol may help the head tremor. Botulinum toxin injection is an option for a disabling head or voice tremor, but neither is disabling now, and voice therapy techniques can steady her sustained notes. [S]

Advanced treatments. Focused ultrasound thalamotomy and deep brain stimulation are for disabling limb tremor that persists after adequate trials of propranolol and primidone. They are not indicated now. [S]

text.paragraph: Data reviewed: Dr. Price's first-visit assessment four weeks ago: TETRAS performance and daily-living subscales, spiral drawing, Timed Up and Go, MoCA 28, and PHQ-9 2; TSH, blood count, and basic chemistry from the same visit, all normal; and today's pulse and seated and standing blood pressure. [S]

list.item: Start propranolol extended-release 60 mg each morning; do not stop it suddenly. [S]

Check resting pulse and seated and 3-minute standing blood pressure at each visit on propranolol, and ask about wheeze, fatigue, low mood, and lightheadedness; repeat the PHQ-9 after three months. [S]

If the hand tremor still limits her after a fair trial, raise propranolol as the pulse allows, or add primidone at 12.5 to 25 mg at bedtime, increased slowly, with checks for sedation and unsteadiness. [S]
Speech-language therapy for the voice tremor. [S]
Occupational therapy for adaptive aids: weighted utensils, a lidded cup, and a thick-barreled pen. [S]
Botulinum toxin injection for the head or voice tremor if either becomes disabling. [S]
No brain imaging or dopamine transporter scan. [S]
Keep caffeine modest, and review any new medicine for tremor-worsening effects. [S]
Refer for focused ultrasound thalamotomy or deep brain stimulation only if disabling limb tremor persists after adequate trials of propranolol and primidone. [S]
Primary care follows her every three to six months with TETRAS, spiral drawing, pulse, standing blood pressure, side effects, and falls. [S]

Discussed with Dr. Price, who sees her the same day. The diagnosis and plan were explained to Ms. Hepburn, who was glad to hear plainly that this is not Parkinson's disease and agreed to the plan. [S]
Follow-up: Movement disorders review in one year, or sooner if the tremor worsens, propranolol is not tolerated, or any sign beyond tremor appears. [S]
